study.title: Matthew 15 - Human tradition, inner purity, mercy to the Gentiles, and abundant provision
study.overview: Matthew 15 shows Jesus confronting the external religion that replaces God's commandment with human rules, teaching that true uncleanness is born from the heart and not from ritual contact with food. Then the chapter opens an important window to God's mercy reaching a Canaanite woman whose persevering faith receives an answer. Finally, Jesus heals many sick people and feeds four thousand men with seven loaves and few little fish, revealing compassion, power, and provision. The closure in Magdala marks the continuation of Jesus' mission after dismissing the crowds.

outline.title: Confrontation with the tradition that nullifies the commandment
outline.explanation: Scribes and Pharisees question the disciples because they did not follow the custom of washing their hands. Jesus responds that their tradition, rather than protecting the will of God, ends up nullifying the commandment to honor father and mother. He calls them hypocrites and quotes Isaiah to show that the religion of lips, without heart, is useless.

outline.title: What really contaminates the human being
outline.explanation: Jesus teaches the multitude that impurity comes not from the food that enters through the mouth, but from what comes from the heart and goes out of the mouth. To the disciples, he explains that the offensic leaders are blind leading blind. The focus of teaching is moral and spiritual: thoughts and words reveal inner corruption.

outline.title: The faith of the Canaanite woman and the mercy that reaches the outside of Israel
outline.explanation: Jesus goes to the region of Tyre and Sidon, where a Canaanite woman cries out for mercy for her demon-sealed daughter. Even in the face of the initial silence and answers that test her perseverance, she insists with humility and confidence. Jesus declares her faith great and heals her daughter from a distance.

outline.title: Mass cures and the multiplication of the loaves
outline.explanation: Back in the region of Galilee, Jesus heals multitudes of sick people and the people glorifies the God of Israel. Then, having mercy on the crowd who had been with him three days ago, feeding four thousand men with seven loaves and some fish, leaving seven baskets left. The chapter ends with Jesus dismissing the crowds and entering a boat to Magdala.

study.context: The notes highlight that the Pharisees come from Jerusalem, where the temple was, and therefore the center of Jewish authority, which gave them weight in their accusation. They also show that the oral tradition of the elders sought to apply the written Law to everyday situations, and that the case of handwashing was treated as a sign of religious fidelity. As for the final destination, there is textual and geographical uncertainty about Magdala, also mentioned as Magadã in some handwritten traditions and associated by some commentators to another next name.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that fidelity to God cannot be replaced by human traditions, even if they have the appearance of religious zeal. Jesus exposes that true purity is moral and spiritual: evil is born from the heart, and the mouth only reveals what already exists within. The Canaanite woman shows that genuine faith perseveres in humiliation, recognizing the authority and compassion of Jesus even when there seems to be a distance between promise and need. The healings and multiplication of the loaves reveal Christ as a prophet, a doctor and pastor, sufficient for the body and for the soul; at the same time, the welcome of the Gentile woman anticipates that God's mercy will not be limited to Israel. In Protestant evangelical reading, the text also confronts any religiosity that prefers external appearance to obedient repentance and faith.

scholarViews.insight: The mention of Jerusalem reinforces the authority of the accusers, because it was the place of the temple and the Jewish religious center; this explains why the delegation came so much weight to confront Jesus.

Jesus calls the crowd and teaches that the problem is not the lack of ritual washing, but what proceeds from within the person; his teaching corrects the dispute over traditions and shifts the focus to true moral contamination.

The closure in Magdala is treated with caution, because the comment observes that the name is uncertain and possibly related to another form preserved in manuscripts; therefore, the exact location should not be affirmed with excess certainty.

questions: In which areas can I be valuing religious custom or personal preference above God's clear commandment?
What words, attitudes and thoughts have revealed the state of my heart before God and of people?
The faith of the Canaanite woman teaches me to persevere even when God seems silent; have I prayed like this?
study.practice: Examine your life in the light of the chapter: abandon any religious practice that only maintains appearance, without real obedience; ask God to purify the heart before trying to correct only external behaviors. Exercise a persevering faith like that of the Canaanite woman, bringing Christ concrete needs with humility and confidence. And practice compassion like that of Jesus, serving tired, wounded or needy people with what you have, without underestimating the provision of God.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text provided features Magdala in verse 39, while the notes indicate textual uncertainty and identify the place as unknown or possibly related to another form of name in manuscripts. It is also important to note that some observations of the commentators are interpretative, especially about the symbolic scope of certain statements of Jesus; they should be read as explanatory readings, not as incontestable conclusions of the text itself.
